title: Exposure to artificial light at night accelerates seasonal reproductive development and nocturnal activity but not migratory departure in a North American songbird
content:
Abstract
Life evolved under dark nights but is now exposed to artificial light at night (ALAN). Many temperate zone organisms rely on photoperiod as a primary cue to initiate seasonal events; consequently, ALAN may disrupt seasonal timing by mimicking longer daylengths. If migratory birds interpret ALAN as longer days, then ALAN exposure may accelerate seasonal timing of migration and reproduction. We exposed captive dark-eyed juncos (Junco hyemalis), a nocturnal migrant that breeds in boreal forests and overwinters in the eastern US, to either ALAN (1.7 lux) or dark nights during early spring. We hypothesized that if ALAN is interpreted as longer days, then seasonal preparation to migrate and reproduce would be affected. We measured proxies for migratory behaviour and physiology, predicting that ALAN birds would exhibit nocturnal migratory restlessness (Zugunruhe) and elevated testosterone sooner than controls. We also predicted that ALAN would suppress night-time melatonin. Because some of these variables co-vary with migratory distance, we anticipated a modulatory role of breeding latitude as indicated by feather stable isotope values. We also predicted that upon release, the ALAN-exposed birds would migrate sooner than controls. Consistent with predictions, we found earlier expression of Zugunruhe in ALAN-exposed birds. We found earlier elevation of testosterone levels in ALAN-exposed males, but did not find suppressed night-time melatonin in ALAN-exposed females. We also did not find that ALAN influenced migratory departure, nor was departure date predicted by fat deposition, sex, or migratory distance. Rather, all birds departed around the same date, and weather was the key determinant of departure date. We discuss whether the lack of effect of ALAN on departure was a consequence of return to natural daylengths after release, thus ending exposure to ALAN. Because spring weather is highly variable from year to year, ALAN may play a role in departure timing under different weather.
